**Delphi** () is a city in and the [county seat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_seat "County seat") of [Carroll County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carroll_County,_Indiana "Carroll County, Indiana"), in the [U.S. state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") of [Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana "Indiana").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphi,_Indiana#cite_note-GR6-6) Located twenty minutes northeast of [Lafayette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lafayette,_Indiana "Lafayette, Indiana"), it is part of the Lafayette, Indiana [Metropolitan Statistical Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lafayette,_Indiana_metropolitan_area "Lafayette, Indiana metropolitan area"). The population was 2,961 at the [2020 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census").
Delphi was [platted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plat "Plat") in 1828.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphi,_Indiana#cite_note-7) It took its name from the ancient city of [Delphi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphi "Delphi"), in Greece.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphi,_Indiana#cite_note-8) Several months after Delphi was founded, it was designated as the county seat.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphi,_Indiana#cite_note-9)

The [Barnett-Seawright-Wilson House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnett-Seawright-Wilson_House "Barnett-Seawright-Wilson House"), [Carroll County Courthouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carroll_County_Courthouse_(Indiana) "Carroll County Courthouse (Indiana)"), [Delphi City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphi_City_Hall "Delphi City Hall"), [Delphi Courthouse Square Historic District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphi_Courthouse_Square_Historic_District "Delphi Courthouse Square Historic District"), [Delphi Methodist Episcopal Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphi_Methodist_Episcopal_Church "Delphi Methodist Episcopal Church"), [Foreman-Case House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreman-Case_House "Foreman-Case House"), and [Niewerth Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niewerth_Building "Niewerth Building") are listed on the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphi,_Indiana#cite_note-nris-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphi,_Indiana#cite_note-nps-11)
Local heritage centers on the [Wabash and Erie Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wabash_and_Erie_Canal "Wabash and Erie Canal"), a canal and [towpath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Towpath "Towpath") that once bound together northern, central, and southern Indiana. The segment of the canal that passes through Delphi has been rewatered and serves as the focus of canal activities. A visitor center and museum, the [Wabash & Erie Canal Interpretive Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wabash_&_Erie_Canal_Interpretive_Center "Wabash & Erie Canal Interpretive Center"), welcomes guests.

There were 1,182 households in Delphi, of which 30.9% had children under the age of 18 living in them. Of all households, 40.7% were married-couple households, 19.5% were households with a male householder and no spouse or partner present, and 30.5% were households with a female householder and no spouse or partner present. About 33.0% of all households were made up of individuals and 13.4% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphi,_Indiana#cite_note-Census2020DP-14)
There were 1,325 housing units, of which 10.8% were vacant. The homeowner vacancy rate was 2.6% and the rental vacancy rate was 8.6%.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphi,_Indiana#cite_note-Census2020DP-14)

**Delphi** ( or ; [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language"): Δελφοί, [[ðelˈfi]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Greek "Help:IPA/Greek")) is a town in [Phocis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phocis "Phocis"), [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece "Greece"), situated immediately west of the [archaeological site of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphi "Delphi"). It was created as a home for the population of [Kastri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kastri,_Phocis "Kastri, Phocis"), which was relocated to allow for the excavation of the site of ancient Delphi. The importance of the twin locations grew to the point where Delphi has also been made the name of the modern-day municipality, which includes the communities of the [Pleistos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pleistos "Pleistos") valley system as far south as the [Gulf of Corinth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Corinth "Gulf of Corinth"). The name Delphi came from the [Oracle of Delphi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythia "Pythia"), which was anciently accepted as a purveyor of truth revealed by the god [Apollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo "Apollo").

The twin sites are on [Greek National Road 48](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_National_Road_48 "Greek National Road 48") linking [Amfissa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amfissa "Amfissa") with [Livadeia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livadeia "Livadeia"). The town contains extensive facilities supporting the tourist trade at the ancient site. Like the ancient Sacred Precinct, the town preserves a vertical dimension by terracing the streets and buildings. The streets are narrow, and often one-way. The [E4 European long distance path](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E4_European_long_distance_path "E4 European long distance path") passes through the east end of the town. In addition to the archaeological interest, Delphi attracts tourists visiting the [Parnassus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Parnassus "Mount Parnassus") Ski Center and the popular coastal towns of the region.
Occupation of the site at Delphi can be traced back to the [Neolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic "Neolithic") period with extensive occupation and use beginning in the Mycenaean period (1600–1100 BC).
Earlier myths [[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphi_(modern_town)#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphi_(modern_town)#cite_note-Harissis_2019-4) include traditions that [Pythia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythia "Pythia"), or the Delphic oracle, already was the site of an important oracle in the pre-classical Greek world (as early as 1400 BC) and, rededicated from about 800 BC, when it served as the major site during classical times for the worship of the god [Apollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo "Apollo").

One account holds that the city was named after the mythological figure of [Lamia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamia_(daughter_of_Poseidon) "Lamia (daughter of Poseidon)"), the daughter of [Poseidon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poseidon "Poseidon") and queen of the Trachineans. Another account holds that it is named after the Malians, the inhabitants of the surrounding area. In the Middle Ages, Lamia was called **Zetounion** (Ζητούνιον), a name first encountered in the [8th Ecumenical Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Council_of_Constantinople_(Roman_Catholic) "Fourth Council of Constantinople (Roman Catholic)") in 869. It was known as **Girton** under [Frankish rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frangokratia "Frangokratia") following the [Fourth Crusade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Crusade "Fourth Crusade") and later **El Citó** when it was controlled by the [Catalan Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan_Company "Catalan Company") of mercenaries. In [Turkish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_language "Turkish language"), it was sometimes called **İzdin** or **İzzeddin**.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamia_(city)#cite_note-3) The city was also known as Zeitoun.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamia_(city)#cite_note-4)
[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/Lamia_pude%C5%82ka_na_kosztownosci.jpg/250px-Lamia_pude%C5%82ka_na_kosztownosci.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lamia_pude%C5%82ka_na_kosztownosci.jpg)
Exhibits at the archaeological museum of the city

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/The_fortress_of_Lamia%2C_1917.jpg/250px-The_fortress_of_Lamia%2C_1917.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_fortress_of_Lamia,_1917.jpg)
Postcard of Lamia, 1917.
[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5c/Pl._Eleftherias_-_Lamia.jpg/250px-Pl._Eleftherias_-_Lamia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pl._Eleftherias_-_Lamia.jpg)
Eleftherias Square
Archaeological excavations have shown the site of Lamia to have been inhabited since at least the [Bronze Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age "Bronze Age") (3rd millennium BC).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamia_(city)#cite_note-ODYSSEUS-5)
In antiquity, the city played an important role due to its strategic location, controlling the narrow coastal plain above [Thermopylae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermopylae "Thermopylae") that connected southern Greece with [Thessaly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thessaly "Thessaly") and the rest of the [Balkans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkans "Balkans"). In its ancient phase, Lamia was located closer to the sea, which explains the existence of the nearby temple dedicated to [Poseidon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poseidon "Poseidon"). With the flow of the [Spercheios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spercheios "Spercheios") river, the terrain changed and the sealine was dragged to the interior of the [Malian Gulf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malian_Gulf "Malian Gulf") -this geological phenomenon altered the straights of [Thermopylae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermopylae "Thermopylae"), too.

**Lamia** ([Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language"): Λαμία, _Lamía_, pronounced[[laˈmi.a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Greek "Help:IPA/Greek")) is a city in [central Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Greece_(geographic_region) "Central Greece (geographic region)"). The city dates back to antiquity, and is today the capital of the [regional unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_units_of_Greece "Regional units of Greece") of [Phthiotis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phthiotis "Phthiotis") and of the [Central Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Greece_(administrative_region) "Central Greece (administrative region)") region (comprising five regional units). According to the 2021 census, the Municipality of Lamia has a population of 66,657, while Lamia itself has 47,529 inhabitants. The city is located on the slopes of [Mount Othrys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Othrys "Mount Othrys"), near the river [Spercheios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spercheios "Spercheios"). It serves as the agricultural center of a fertile rural and livestock area.

**Epidaurus** ([Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language"): Ἐπίδαυρος) was a small city (_[polis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polis "Polis")_) in [ancient Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greece "Ancient Greece"), on the [Argolid Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argolid_Peninsula "Argolid Peninsula") at the [Saronic Gulf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saronic_Gulf "Saronic Gulf"). Two modern towns bear the name Epidavros: _[Palaia Epidavros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palaia\_Epidavros "Palaia Epidavros")_ and _[Nea Epidavros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nea\_Epidavros "Nea Epidavros")_. Since 2010 they belong to the new municipality of Epidaurus, part of the regional unit of [Argolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argolis "Argolis"). The seat of the municipality is the town [Lygourio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lygourio "Lygourio").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epidaurus#cite_note-Kallikratis-2) The nearby [sanctuary of Asclepius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_Asclepius,_Epidaurus "Temple of Asclepius, Epidaurus") and [ancient theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Theatre_of_Epidaurus "Ancient Theatre of Epidaurus") were inscribed on the [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO")[World Heritage List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_List "World Heritage List") in 1988 because of their exemplary architecture and importance in the development and spread of healing sanctuaries and cults across the ancient Greek and Roman worlds.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epidaurus#cite_note-unesco-3)

The name "Epidaurus" is of [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language") origin. It was named after the hero [Epidauros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epidaurus_(mythology) "Epidaurus (mythology)"), son of [Apollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo "Apollo").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epidaurus#cite_note-4) According to [Strabo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strabo "Strabo"), the city was originally named Ἐπίκαρος (Epíkaros) under the [Carians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carians "Carians"), ([Aristotle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle") claimed that [Caria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caria "Caria"), as a naval empire, occupied Epidaurus and Hermione)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epidaurus#cite_note-5) before taking the name Ἐπίταυρος (Epítauros) when the city was taken by the [Ionians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionians "Ionians") and finally becoming Ἐπίδαυρος (Epídauros) after the [Dorians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorians "Dorians") conquered the city. Compare the individual elements ἐπί (epí, "upon"), Καρία (Karía, "Carian"), ταῦρος (taûros, "bull") and Δωριεύς (Dōrieús "Dorian")/Δωριεῖς (Dōrieîs, "Dorians").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epidaurus#cite_note-6)

Epidaurus was independent of [Argos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Argos "Ancient Argos") and not included in [Argolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argolis "Argolis") until the time of the [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome"). With its supporting territory, it formed the small territory called [Epidauria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epidauria "Epidauria"). It was reputed to be founded by or named for the hero [Epidaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epidaurus_(mythology) "Epidaurus (mythology)"), and to be the birthplace of [Apollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo "Apollo")'s son [Asclepius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asclepius "Asclepius") the healer.

Athens[a] is the capital and largest city of Greece. A significant coastal urban area in the Mediterranean, Athens is also the capital of the Attica region and is the southernmost capital on the European mainland. With its urban area's population numbering over 3.6 million, it is the eighth-largest urban area in the European Union (EU). The Municipality of Athens (also City of Athens), which constitutes a small administrative unit of the entire urban area, had a population of 643,452 in 2021,[4] within its official limits, and a land area of 38.96 square kilometres (15.04 square miles).[7][8] Athens joined the UNESCO Global Network of Learning Cities in 2016.[9]
Athens is one of the world's oldest cities, with its recorded history spanning over 3,400 years,[10] and its earliest human presence beginning somewhere between the 11th and 7th millennia BC. According to Greek mythology, the city was named after Athena, the ancient Greek goddess of wisdom, but modern scholars generally agree that the goddess took her name after the city.[11] Classical Athens was one of the most powerful city-states in ancient Greece. It was a centre for Ancient Greek democracy, the arts, education and philosophy,[12][13] and was highly influential throughout the Hellenistic world and the European continent, particularly in ancient Rome.[14] For this reason it is often regarded as the cradle of Western civilisation and the birthplace of democracy in its own right independently from the rest of Greece.[15][16]

In modern times Athens is a large cosmopolitan metropolis and central to economic, financial, industrial, maritime, political and cultural life in Greece. It is a Beta (+) – status global city according to the Globalization and World Cities Research Network,[17] and is one of the biggest economic centres in Southeast Europe. It also has a large financial sector, and its port Piraeus is both the second-busiest passenger port in Europe[18] and the thirteenth-largest container port in the world.[19] The Athens metropolitan area[20] extends beyond its administrative municipal city limits as well as its urban agglomeration, with a population of 3,638,281 in 2021[4][21][22] over an area of 2,928.717 km2 (1,131 sq mi).[8]
The heritage of the Classical Era is still evident in the city, represented by ancient monuments, and works of art, the most famous of these being the Parthenon, considered a key landmark of early Western culture. Athens retains Roman, Byzantine and a smaller number of Ottoman monuments, while its historical urban core features elements of continuity through its millennia of history. Athens contains two World Heritage Sites recognised by UNESCO: the Acropolis of Athens and the medieval Daphni Monastery. Athens is home to several museums and cultural institutions, such as the National Archeological Museum, featuring the world's largest collection of ancient Greek antiquities, the Acropolis Museum, the Museum of Cycladic Art, the Benaki Museum and the Byzantine and Christian Museum. Athens was the host city of the first modern-day Olympic Games in 1896, and 108 years later it hosted the 2004 Summer Olympics, making it one of five cities to have hosted the Summer Olympics on more than one occasion.[23]

Its decorative sculptures are considered some of the high points of classical [Greek art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_in_Ancient_Greece "Art in Ancient Greece"), and the Parthenon is considered an enduring symbol of [ancient Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greece "Ancient Greece"), [Western civilisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_culture "Western culture"), and [democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy "Democracy").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthenon#cite_note-Beard2010-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthenon#cite_note-:2-9)
The Parthenon was built in the 5th century BC in thanksgiving for the Greek victory over the [Persian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achaemenid_Empire "Achaemenid Empire") invaders during the [Greco-Persian Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greco-Persian_Wars "Greco-Persian Wars").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthenon#cite_note-:0-10) Like most Greek temples, the Parthenon also served as the city [treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treasury "Treasury").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthenon#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthenon#cite_note-12) Construction started in 447 BC when the [Delian League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delian_League "Delian League") was at the peak of its power. It was completed in 438 BC; work on the artwork and decorations continued until 432 BC. For a time, it served as the treasury of the Delian League, which later became the [Athenian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athenian_Empire "Athenian Empire").

Tourism is a significant economic sector.[127][128][129] The presence of natural attractions like beaches, backwaters, hills, and plantations and attractions like heritage, history, Ayurveda, medical tourism and knowledge centres attract many tourists.[130] The city experienced a surge of investment in the real estate, infrastructure and retail sectors in 2016–17.[131]
Port-based developmentedit
Thiruvananthapuram is a commercial port city with port-related infrastructure due to the presence of the Deepwater Container Transhipment port operated by the Vizhinjam International Seaport Ltd. Thiruvananthapuram.[132]
The port is located close to international shipping routes, approximately 10 to 12 nautical miles (19 to 22 km) from the busy Persian Gulf–Malacca shipping lane.[133] It has a natural depth of 18 to 20 metres (59 to 66 ft), enabling it to accommodate large container vessels.[134] The berths are designed to handle vessels of up to 24,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEU).[135] Port-related development has been associated with increased activity in logistics, warehousing, shipping services and supporting infrastructure, trade and transport connectivity.[citation needed]
Trivandrum Outer Ring Roadedit

The proposed Trivandrum Outer Ring Road (ORR) (ORR), also known as the Outer Area Growth Corridor (OAGC), is a major infrastructure initiative aimed at supporting the long-term economic development of the city and its surrounding region. The corridor, extending approximately 78–80 km between Vizhinjam International Seaport Thiruvananthapuram and Navaikulam, is planned as a six-lane access-controlled highway with designated economic zones along its alignment. The TOAGC master plan envisages the development of multiple sector-specific clusters, including logistics, industrial development, information technology, healthcare, health tourism, general tourism, education, and commercial services, forming an integrated investment region around the capital area. Key nodes such as Vizhinjam, Kovalam, Vembayam, Mangalapuram, and Nedumangad have been identified for focused development, including a logistics hub at Vizhinjam and a health and tourism hub in the coastal belt. The project is also expected to strengthen connectivity between Vizhinjam International Seaport, the IT corridors, and the national highway network, thereby facilitating port-led industrial growth and regional economic expansion.[136][137][138]

Thiruvananthapuram is a major tourist hub in India.[128] Kovalam and Varkala are popular beach towns near the city.[139] Other important beaches include Poovar, Shankumugham Beach, Azhimala Beach, Vizhinjam Beach and Veli Beach. Other places of interest include the Agasthyamala rain forests, Neyyar Wildlife Sanctuary, Kallar, Braemore, Ponmudi hills, Poovar, the Anchuthengu backwaters, Varkala Cliffs and Kappil-Edava lakes. [citation needed]
The city is also known for its unique style of architecture involving Kerala Architecture with British and Dravidian influences.[140] Napier museum, Thiruvanathapuram Zoo, Padmanabha Swamy temple, Kuthira Malika palace, Kilimanoor palace and The Thiruvananthapuram Golf Club heritage building are examples of this. Cultureedit  
Main article: Culture of Thiruvananthapuram  
Established in 1855, the Napier Museum contains a vast collection of Ancient paintings and archaeological artefacts
Thiruvananthapuram is known as the "Evergreen City of India" because of its green landscapes and the presence of many public parks.[142] Thiruvananthapuram has historically been a cultural hub in Southern India due to the development of arts, architecture and liberal customs by the rulers of erstwhile Thiruvananthapuram. As a testimony to this, renowned artists like Maharaja Swathi Thirunal and Raja Ravi Varma hail from the city.[143][144] Prominent social reformers such as Sri Narayana Guru, Chattampi Swamikal, Ayyankali, Vakkom Moulavi and C. V. Raman Pillai also are from Thiruvananthapuram.[145]

Two of the three Malayalam triumvirate poets, Ulloor S. Parameswara Iyer and Kumaran Asan are from Thiruvananthapuram.[146][147] Annual literature festivals like the Kovalam Literary Festival, are held in the city.[148] Literary development is further aided by state institutions such as the State Central Library, one of the oldest public libraries in India, which was established in 1829,[149] and other major libraries including the Thiruvananthapuram Corporation Central library, and the Kerala University Library.[150] Thiruvananthapuram has been a hub of classical music since the days of Maharaja of Travancore, Swathi Thirunal.[151][152] Thiruvananthapuram is known for many music festivals like the Navarathri Music Festival, one of the oldest festivals of its kind in South India,[151] Swathi Sangeethotsavam, Soorya Music fest, Neelakanta Sivan Music Fest and many other music festivals are organised by various cultural groups.[151] The 111-day-long Soorya Festival is the biggest art and cultural event in Kerala.[153][154] The Soorya Festival features film festivals, theatre festivals, dance, music, painting and photography exhibitions.[153]

The city takes its name from the Malayalam word thiru-anantha-puram (തിരുവനന്തപുരം [t̪iɾuʋɐnɐn̪d̪ɐpuɾɐm] ⓘ), meaning "The City of Lord Anantha (means infinite, endless, or eternal)",[30] referring to the deity of the Sri Padmanabhaswamy Temple located in the city. Thiruvananthapuram is also known in literature, and popular reference as Ananthapuri, derived from the Sanskrit word Syanandurapuram, meaning "The City of Bliss" in Carnatic kirtanas composed by Swathi Thirunal, erstwhile Maharaja of Travancore.[31] The city was officially referred to as Trivandrum until 1991 (Trivandrum being the anglicised name of the town), when the government decided to reinstate the city's original name Thiruvananthapuram. Many Malayalees still refer to the city as Trivandrum, however.[32] The city was also called as Anandapatnam or Anandapatam in Tamil and Telugu, meaning "The City of Ananda" which has the same meaning as the original name. Pre-historic periodedit

Thiruvananthapuram is a relatively modern region with trading traditions dating back to 1000 BCE.[33][34] It is believed that the ships of King Solomon landed in a port then called Ophir (now Poovar) in Thiruvananthapuram in 1036 BCE.[35][36] The city was the trading post for spices, sandalwood and ivory.[37] However, the ancient political and cultural history of the city was almost entirely independent from that of the rest of Kerala. [citation needed]
Ancient periodedit
The southern region of present-day Kerala state (The coastal belt between Thiruvananthapuram and Alappuzha) was under the Ay dynasty, which was more related to the Pandya dynasty of Madurai.[38][page needed] The early rulers of the city were the Ays. Vizhinjam, which is now a region in present-day Thiruvananthapuram, was the capital of the Ay dynasty.[39] Vizhinjam was an important port city from as early as the second century BC.[40][41] During the Ay dynasty's rule, Thiruvananthapuram witnessed many battles in which the Chola and Pandyan dynasties attempted to capture the port town.[42][43]
Middle Agesedit
After the death of king Vikramaditya Varaguna in 925 AD, the glory of the Ays departed and almost all their territories became part of the Chera dynasty.[44][19] During the tenth century, the Cholas attacked and sacked Vizhinjam and surrounding regions.[19] The port in Vizhinjam and the historic education centre of Kanthalloor Sala were also destroyed by Cholas during this period.[45][46] A branch of the Ay family, which had controlled the Padmanabhaswamy Temple, merged with the Kingdom of Venad in the 12th century.[19]

Located on the west coast of India near the extreme south of the mainland, Thiruvananthapuram is a port city located 10 nautical miles (19 km; 12 mi)[15] from a heavily trafficked east–west shipping channel. The city is home to India's first deep-water trans-shipment port, owned by the Vizhinjam International Seaport Ltd. Thiruvananthapuram under the Government of Kerala.[16] The city is characterised by its undulating terrain of low coastal hills.[17] Thiruvananthapuram is also known for its cultural heritage, being associated with the musical contributions of Swathi Thirunal Rama Varma and the artistic legacy of painter Raja Ravi Varma. Thiruvananthapuram has contributed to the development of Malayalam literature through individuals like Ulloor S. Parameswara Iyer, Kumaran Asan, C. V. Raman Pillai and Narayana Guru. The city is also known for Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple, known as the richest temple in the world.[18] The other temples includes the Sreevaraham temple, the Shreekanteswaram temple and the Attukal Bhagavathy temple.
The present regions that constitute Thiruvananthapuram were ruled by the Ays who were related to feudatories of the Chera dynasty.[19] In the 12th century, it was conquered by the Kingdom of Venad.[19] In the 18th century, the king Marthanda Varma expanded the territory, founded the princely state of Travancore and made Thiruvananthapuram its capital.[20] Travancore became the most dominant state in Kerala by defeating the powerful Zamorin of Calicut in the battle of Purakkad in 1755.[21] Following India's independence in 1947, Thiruvananthapuram became the capital of Travancore–Cochin state and remained so until the new Indian state of Kerala was formed in 1956.[22][23]

Thiruvananthapuram is a notable academic and research hub and home to the University of Kerala, APJ Abdul Kalam Technological University, the regional headquarters of Indira Gandhi National Open University, and many other schools and colleges. Thiruvananthapuram is also home to research centres such as the National Institute for Interdisciplinary Science and Technology, the Indian Space Research Organisation's Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre, the Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology, the National Centre for Earth Science Studies and a campus of the Indian Institutes of Science Education and Research.[24] Thiruvananthapuram is where India's space programme began, with the headquarters of Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre located there. The city is home to media institutions like Toonz Animation India and Tata Elxsi Ltd, and also to Chitranjali Film Studio, one of the first film studios in Malayalam Cinema, and Kinfra Film and Video Park at Kazhakoottam, which is India's first infotainment industrial park.[25]
In 2012, Thiruvananthapuram was named the best Kerala city to live in, by a field survey conducted by The Times of India.[26] In 2013, the city was ranked the fifteenth best city to live in in India, in a survey conducted by India Today.[27] Thiruvananthapuram was ranked the best Indian city for two consecutive years, 2015 and 2016, according to the Annual Survey of India's City-Systems (ASICS) conducted by the Janaagraha Centre for Citizenship and Democracy.[28] The city was also selected as the best governed city in India in a survey conducted by Janaagraha Centre for citizenship and democracy in 2017.[29]

Thiruvananthapuram is a notable academic and research hub and home to the University of Kerala, APJ Abdul Kalam Technological University, the regional headquarters of Indira Gandhi National Open University, and many other schools and colleges. Thiruvananthapuram is also home to research centres such as the National Institute for Interdisciplinary Science and Technology, the Indian Space Research Organisation's Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre, the Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology, the National Centre for Earth Science Studies and a campus of the Indian Institutes of Science Education and Research.[24] Thiruvananthapuram is where India's space programme began, with the headquarters of Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre located there. The city is home to media institutions like Toonz Animation India and Tata Elxsi Ltd, and also to Chitranjali Film Studio, one of the first film studios in Malayalam Cinema, and Kinfra Film and Video Park at Kazhakoottam, which is India's first infotainment industrial park.[25]
In 2012, Thiruvananthapuram was named the best Kerala city to live in, by a field survey conducted by The Times of India.[26] In 2013, the city was ranked the fifteenth best city to live in in India, in a survey conducted by India Today.[27] Thiruvananthapuram was ranked the best Indian city for two consecutive years, 2015 and 2016, according to the Annual Survey of India's City-Systems (ASICS) conducted by the Janaagraha Centre for Citizenship and Democracy.[28] The city was also selected as the best governed city in India in a survey conducted by Janaagraha Centre for citizenship and democracy in 2017.[29]
Etymologyedit

The city takes its name from the Malayalam word thiru-anantha-puram (തിരുവനന്തപുരം [t̪iɾuʋɐnɐn̪d̪ɐpuɾɐm] ⓘ), meaning "The City of Lord Anantha (means infinite, endless, or eternal)",[30] referring to the deity of the Sri Padmanabhaswamy Temple located in the city. Thiruvananthapuram is also known in literature, and popular reference as Ananthapuri, derived from the Sanskrit word Syanandurapuram, meaning "The City of Bliss" in Carnatic kirtanas composed by Swathi Thirunal, erstwhile Maharaja of Travancore.[31] The city was officially referred to as Trivandrum until 1991 (Trivandrum being the anglicised name of the town), when the government decided to reinstate the city's original name Thiruvananthapuram. Many Malayalees still refer to the city as Trivandrum, however.[32] The city was also called as Anandapatnam or Anandapatam in Tamil and Telugu, meaning "The City of Ananda" which has the same meaning as the original name. [citation needed]
Historyedit  
Main article: History of Thiruvananthapuram  
See also: Merger of Kanyakumari with Madras State  
Painting by Raja Ravi Varma depicting Richard Temple-Grenville, 3rd Duke of Buckingham and Chandos being greeted by Visakham Thirunal, with Ayilyam Thirunal of Travancore looking on, during Buckingham's visit to Thiruvananthapuram in early 1880  
Padmanabhaswamy Temple is the richest temple in the world.  
Padmanabhapuram Palace  
Pre-historic periodedit

Thiruvananthapuram is a relatively modern region with trading traditions dating back to 1000 BCE.[33][34] It is believed that the ships of King Solomon landed in a port then called Ophir (now Poovar) in Thiruvananthapuram in 1036 BCE.[35][36] The city was the trading post for spices, sandalwood and ivory.[37] However, the ancient political and cultural history of the city was almost entirely independent from that of the rest of Kerala. [citation needed]
Ancient periodedit
The southern region of present-day Kerala state (The coastal belt between Thiruvananthapuram and Alappuzha) was under the Ay dynasty, which was more related to the Pandya dynasty of Madurai.[38][page needed] The early rulers of the city were the Ays. Vizhinjam, which is now a region in present-day Thiruvananthapuram, was the capital of the Ay dynasty.[39] Vizhinjam was an important port city from as early as the second century BC.[40][41] During the Ay dynasty's rule, Thiruvananthapuram witnessed many battles in which the Chola and Pandyan dynasties attempted to capture the port town.[42][43]
Middle Agesedit
After the death of king Vikramaditya Varaguna in 925 AD, the glory of the Ays departed and almost all their territories became part of the Chera dynasty.[44][19] During the tenth century, the Cholas attacked and sacked Vizhinjam and surrounding regions.[19] The port in Vizhinjam and the historic education centre of Kanthalloor Sala were also destroyed by Cholas during this period.[45][46] A branch of the Ay family, which had controlled the Padmanabhaswamy Temple, merged with the Kingdom of Venad in the 12th century.[19]

Thiruvananthapuram district is located between [8°10′N 76°25′E / 8.17°N 76.41°E](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Thiruvananthapuram_district&params=8.17_N_76.41_E_) and [8°32′N 77°10′E / 8.54°N 77.17°E](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Thiruvananthapuram_district&params=8.54_N_77.17_E_). At the southernmost extremity of the district, Kaliyikkavila is 54 kilometres (34 mi) from [Kanyakumari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanyakumari "Kanyakumari"), the southernmost point on the Indian peninsula.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_district#cite_note-14) 33.75% of the district population lives in urban areas.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_district#cite_note-15)

The district has three major rivers, several freshwater lakes, and over 300 ponds. Its eastern region is forested, northern regions are mostly under rubber cultivation and the remaining areas grow mixed dry-land crops of coconut, plantain, and tapioca, among others. Built-up areas and rice fields complete the land use pattern.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_district#cite_note-16)
The name Thiruvananthapuram, shared by the district and its headquarters city, comes from the [Malayalam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malayalam "Malayalam")/[Tamil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamil_language "Tamil language") word "Thiru" and [Sanskrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit_language "Sanskrit language") word "anantha-pura", meaning "Abode of Lord Anantha".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram_district#cite_note-Meaning_of_name-17) The name derives from the deity of the [Hindu temple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu_temple "Hindu temple") at the center of Thiruvananthapuram city. Anantha is another name of Vishnu, the deity of [Sree Padmanabhaswamy temple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sree_Padmanabhaswamy_temple "Sree Padmanabhaswamy temple"). The district's official name in English was Trivandrum until 1991, when the government reinstated the city's original name, Thiruvananthapuram, in all languages.

## Shashi Tharoor, a former UN diplomat, began his journey in electoral politics, winning Thiruvananthapuram in the 2009 Lok Sabha polls.

The electoral battle in Thiruvananthapuram is all flared up for a high-stakes face-off between senior Congress leader Shashi Tharoor, seeking a fourth consecutive term, and Union Minister Rajeev Chandrasekhar, the Bharatiya Janata Party's (BJP) candidate. For 15 years, the constituency has been inseparable from the name ‘Shashi Tharoor’ as voters have consistently elected the Congress leader to represent them in the Lok Sabha.
Fielding a newbie against a rather popular and people-elect Shashi Tharoor, who has amassed a loyal base over the years, is a significant gamble for the BJP, as it [aims to gain a foothold in Kerala](https://www.livemint.com/politics/news/lok-sabha-elections-2024-5-keenly-watched-contests-in-kerala-can-the-bjp-open-its-account-in-gods-own-country-11714045334694.html).
This raises the question: Does tech-savvy BJP candidate Rajeev Chandrasekhar stand a chance against three-time MP Shashi Tharoor in Thiruvananthapuram? Let's look at how Thiruvananthapuram has voted in the past three Lok Sabha elections.

## THE STORY OF PAST ELECTIONS IN THIRUVANANTHAPURAM
The parliamentary constituency has switched between the Communist Party of India (CPI) and the Congress since 1977, but Shashi Tharoor has come a long way since he first won the Thiruvananthapuram constituency in 2009. Despite the said “Modi wave”, which turned the fate of many big leaders in the country, the impact has been least visible in Thiruvananthapuram.
The Lok Sabha constituency has consistently seen an upward trend in voter turnout during the 2009, 2014, and 2019 elections. In 2009, the voter turnout was 65.74 per cent; in 2014, the turnout increased to 68.63 per cent and in 2019, the voter turnout was recorded at 73.45 per cent.
Although the BJP candidates couldn't unseat Shashi Tharoor in the past two elections, the vote share reflects that they were neck-and-neck with the Congress leader in these elections.

Source: https://www.livemint.com/elections/thiruvananthapuram-lok-sabha-elections-2024-can-rajeev-chandrasekhar-beat-3-time-winner-mp-shashi-tharoor-11714032438568.html
Chunks: 2,3
## HOW THIRUVANANTHAPURAM VOTED IN PAST THREE ELECTIONS
**2009 Lok Sabha elections:** Thiruvananthapuram saw a three-cornered contest between [Congress' Shashi Tharoor](https://www.livemint.com/news/india/if-chandrasekhar-ignores-the-demand-shashi-tharoor-warns-bjp-leader-after-legal-notice-on-defamation-11712887879952.html), who was contesting for the first time from the seat, CPI's P Ramachandran Nair, BSP's A Neelalohithadasan Nadar. Shashi Tharoor won the seat with 326,725 (44.29 per cent votes), defeating CPI's P Ramachandran Nair with a margin of 99,998 votes. The CPI candidate won 226,727 (30.74 per cent votes). The BJP was far behind, winning 84,094 votes.
**2014 Lok Sabha elections:**As India rallied behind Narendra Modi's “_ab ki baar Modi sarkar_”, BJP, too, advanced two steps in the Thiruvananthapuram seat, narrowing the gap in the race with Shashi Tharoor. The BJP increased its vote share by 20.92 per cent from the 2009 elections as Shashi Tharoor's vote share dropped by 10.20 per cent. In a tight race, Shashi Tharoor won 297,806 votes in the 2014 elections, and BJP's seasoned O Rajagopal won 2,82,336 votes. The margin of votes was only 15,470.
**2019 Lok Sabha elections:** Shashi Tharoor won the Thiruvananthapuram seat again with a larger vote margin of 99,989. BJP's Kummanam Rajasekharan was pitted against Shashi Tharoor. The saffron party's total vote share decreased by 1.02 percent, while Congress' increased by 7.10 percent.

## HOW THIRUVANANTHAPURAM VOTED IN PAST THREE ELECTIONS
In an interview with _ANI_ recently, Shashi Tharoor commented on the BJP's campaign in Thiruvananthapuram: “[It's not a surprise that they have turned out to be a strong player](https://www.livemint.com/politics/news/shashi-tharoor-bjp-strong-player-in-thiruvananthapuram-rajeev-chandrasekhar-perception-battle-lok-sabha-election-2024-11712918599118.html). The Communist campaign has been lacklustre, whereas the BJP has moved into the second position in this constituency.”
In the Lok Sabha 2024 elections, Shashi Tharoor is looking to retain the support of his loyal base. The BJP, buoyed by its performance over the years, is eyeing to wrest power from the Congress, placing all its hopes on Rajeev Chandrasekhar,[who has never contested the Lok Sabha elections](https://www.livemint.com/politics/news/lok-sabha-election-2024-shashi-tharoor-vs-rajeev-chandrasekhar-high-octane-poll-battle-likely-in-thiruvananthapuram-11709618797010.html) before.
